title: The five afflictions (2.3)
hook: one short sutra names the five roots of human trouble, in the order they grow
tomorrow: ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent

segments.voice: Yesterday: kriya yoga, three. Discipline, study, surrender, to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions. Did you try one of each? Today, what exactly gets thinned. And the week closes. Day four hundred forty-eight.

A doctor can treat a fever, or find the infection causing it. Most of us spend our lives treating fevers: a flash of anger here, a craving there, a wave of fear at 2am. Patanjali goes looking for the infection. Yesterday he said kriya yoga thins the afflictions. Today, in sutra 2.3, he names them. There are five, and the order is not random. Each one grows out of the one before it, like branches from a trunk.
screen: `TREATING THE FEVER.` → `FINDING THE INFECTION.` → `FIVE ROOTS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.3: avidya asmita raga dvesha abhiniveshah kleshah. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life are the afflictions. Klesha means affliction, a trouble, something that causes pain. Here's the order, quickly, because each gets its own day this week. Avidya, ignorance: not a lack of facts, but seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts. Asmita, I-ness: the sense of a separate me that grows out of that mistake. Raga, attraction: the pull toward what pleased that me. Dvesha, aversion: the push away from what hurt it. Abhinivesha: clinging to life, the deep fear of ending, which Patanjali says is found even in the wise. Read it as a family tree. Misreading reality produces a small, separate self. A separate self wants things and fears things. And underneath all the wanting and fearing runs the will to keep going at any cost. Notice what isn't on the list: no demons, no sins, no bad luck. Just five ways the mind gets reality wrong and then defends the mistake. Now the week, from the top. Day one, many doors. Day two, mastery from the smallest to the largest. Day three, the crystal takes the color. Day four, truth-bearing wisdom. Day five, seedless, the end of chapter one. Day six, kriya yoga, chapter two begins. Today, the five afflictions, the roots that the whole practice is meant to thin.
screen: `KLESHA: AN AFFLICTION.` · `IGNORANCE, THEN I-NESS.` · `ATTRACTION, AVERSION, CLINGING.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `FIVE ROOTS, ONE FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle on the breath. As thoughts come, try sorting them into the five, gently, without fuss. A thought about wanting something: attraction. A thought about avoiding something: aversion. A thought that's all about me, my image, my place: I-ness. A flicker of fear about the future: clinging. You don't need to find ignorance; it's said to be under all of them. Just notice, name, and return. The bell holds the time.
The five afflictions. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life: the kleshas of sutra 2.3, each growing from the one before.
Your line: kleshas. The next time you feel a strong reaction today, ask which of the five it grows from before you act on it. Day four hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 448 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK FROM DOORS TO ROOTS, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: IGNORANCE.`

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five kleshas as the root diagnosis of suffering, and many teachers ask them to trace everyday reactions back to these roots during meditation and daily life.

pairs: clinging to life, even in the wise

myth: avidya means not knowing enough facts
it means seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts.
Patanjali lists five afflictions in sutra 2.3
ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion, clinging to life.
the next sutra calls ignorance the field for the other four.

fork.setup: you snap at a friend over something small. Patanjali would want you to look where?
options: at the root: which affliction it grows from, and beneath it, ignorance.
fork.reveal: 2.3 names five roots. a snap is often aversion, or wounded I-ness, and the next sutra says all of them grow from ignorance.

original.note: Sanskrit kleśa: affliction, a cause of pain. Patanjali names five in 2.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: an affliction is a bad thing that happens to you.
what it means: five ways the mind misreads reality and then defends the mistake.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa calls the kleshas the five kinds of viparyaya, error, linking them back to 1.8; the same diagnostic idea of kleshas also appears in Buddhist thought.
